hops.afterHeading: An epithelial cell that feels force
hops.title: Pig snouts and a 139-year argument over Merkel cells
hops.text: In 1875 the German anatomist Friedrich Merkel put pig snout skin under a light microscope and found large, pale cells at the base of the epidermis, in close contact with nerve endings. He called them Tastzellen, touch cells, presuming they were touch receptors. Then came more than a century of argument. As late as 2003, an Anatomical Record review reported “conclusive evidence” that mammalian Merkel cells came from neural crest. Six years later, two mouse studies traced them to epidermal progenitors instead. In 2014, three mouse and rat studies showed the cells are touch-sensitive through Piezo2. The name Merkel gave them on a hunch held up.

sources.citation: Munde et al., Pathophysiology of Merkel cell, J Oral Maxillofac Pathol (2013), PMC3927344
Halata, Grim & Bauman, Anat Rec A (2003), PMID 12552639
Van Keymeulen et al., J Cell Biol (2009), PMID 19786578; Morrison et al., Dev Biol (2009), PMID 19782676
Woo, Lumpkin & Patapoutian, Merkel cells and neurons keep in touch, Trends Cell Biol (2015), PMC4312710

image.caption: Merkel named them touch cells in 1875. Mouse studies later traced their origin, and rodent studies showed they sense touch.

hops.title: Why a light touch can itch on dry, aging skin
hops.text: Age-related dry skin is strongly associated with alloknesis: itch set off by an ordinarily non-itchy stimulus, such as a light touch. In 2018, Feng and colleagues found that aged mice, and mice with experimentally dried skin, lose Merkel cells from their touch domes while the afferent endings stay intact. Sustained SA1 firing during a hold was reduced, and light touches evoked scratching, including in aged mice tested with filaments of 0.02 to 0.16 gram-force. Deleting Piezo2 from Merkel cells alone also increased touch-evoked scratching, and switching spared Merkel cells on in dry skin reduced it. Merkel-cell signaling appears to help hold mechanical itch in check, perhaps through inhibitory spinal interneurons.

sources.citation: Feng et al., Piezo2 channel-Merkel cell signaling modulates the conversion of touch to itch, Science (2018), PMID 29724954, PMC6114129

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A folded cream wool sweater with a fuzzy collar draped over a sunlit armchair beside a mug of tea.
image.caption: Aged mice and mice with dried skin scratched after light touch and had fewer Merkel cells.

hops.title: Fine and coarse sandpaper under a still fingertip
hops.text: Get two fine sandpapers of slightly different grit and two coarse ones. Rest a fingertip on each without moving, then slide across them. In Hollins and Risner's 2000 experiments, fine abrasive surfaces that people told apart easily when moved across the skin became indistinguishable when held still, while coarse surfaces were just as easy to tell apart either way. Holding still removes the skin vibrations that fine texture depends on, which vibration-sensitive afferents mainly carry. What is left is coarse spatial layout, the kind of information SA1 fibres carry. With your finger still, the fine pair may be much harder to tell apart than the coarse pair.

sources.citation: Hollins & Risner, Evidence for the duplex theory of tactile texture perception, Percept Psychophys (2000), PMID 10883578
Weber et al., Spatial and temporal codes mediate the tactile perception of natural textures, PNAS (2013), PMID 24082087

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A hand on a wooden desk with one fingertip resting on fine grey sandpaper beside a sheet of coarse brown sandpaper.
image.caption: Holding still makes fine textures harder to tell apart, while coarse differences still come through.

audio.title: Braille dots, a missing channel, and a mole's thirty thousand touch organs
audio.transcript:
Three stories about touch at its finest grain: a page of braille, two patients without working Piezo two, and a mole whose nose is built from thirty thousand touch organs.

First, braille. On standard paper braille in the United States and Canada, a cell has six possible dot positions in two columns of three. Within a cell, neighbouring positions in the same row or column are about two point three four millimetres apart, centre to centre, and a raised dot is about half a millimetre high. In the early nineteen nineties, Phillips, Johansson and Johnson recorded single nerve fibres in human fingertips while embossed dots scrolled across the skin. In one experiment, the S A one fibres, the ones paired with Merkel cells, and the rapidly adapting type one fibres resolved dots about one point five millimetres apart. In another, plots rebuilt from the responses of those two fibre types showed braille letters you could recognize by eye. The deeper type two fibres blurred anything closer than about three point five millimetres and did not resolve braille at all. Braille spacing sits comfortably above the limit of the S A one fibres.

Second, how the channel was found, and what happens without it. Ardem Patapoutian's team started with a mouse cell line that gave off an electrical signal when a single cell was poked with a micropipette. They listed seventy-two candidate genes and silenced them one at a time, poking the cells after each knockdown. Eventually, knocking down one gene sharply reduced the current the cells produced when poked. They named it Piezo one, from the Greek word for pressure, and a similar gene, Piezo two, turned out to be expressed at high levels in sensory neurons. In twenty sixteen, Chesler and colleagues at the National Institutes of Health described two patients, a teenager and a child, who carried inactivating variants in the PIEZO2 gene. Neither could feel a tuning fork vibrating at one hundred twenty-eight hertz, even at full amplitude. On the hairless skin of the hand, they were forty percent correct at telling one point from two points ten to thirteen millimetres apart, no better than guessing. With their eyes closed they could not walk, because their sense of joint position was profoundly reduced. Yet when someone slowly brushed the hairy skin of their forearm, both detected it every time. The authors suggest that this gentle, caress-like touch travels on a separate pathway.

Third, the star-nosed mole. This small mammal explores its underground world with a snout ringed by twenty-two fleshy appendages, and those appendages are covered with about thirty thousand tiny bumps called Eimer's organs. Each one holds a column of epidermal cells threaded with nerve endings, a single Merkel cell-neurite complex, and a single lamellated corpuscle just beneath. Catania, who described them, called the star perhaps the most sensitive touch organ yet discovered for its size. Later, Catania and Remple timed the moles identifying and eating prey in as little as a hundred and twenty milliseconds, two hundred twenty-seven on average. The moles even made quick double takes, which the authors read as a sign that they have reached the speed limit for processing touch. It is the same Merkel complex that sits in your fingertip, repeated thirty thousand times across a nose.
